blocks.md: L'Hôpital's rule resolves expressions that collapse to zero divided by zero, or infinity divided by infinity, as some quantity approaches a limit. Instead of the ratio of the two functions, look at the ratio of how fast each is changing — their derivatives — which often has a clear answer. It explains two results you meet in economics: why the log is a special case of the Box-Cox power family, and why the CES production function becomes Cobb-Douglas.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It shows that some special cases are genuine limits of a family rather than separate assumptions.
If $f(a) = g(a) = 0$ (or both tend to $\pm\infty$) and the limit on the right exists:
Other indeterminate forms ($0\cdot\infty$, $1^\infty$, $\infty - \infty$) are rewritten as a ratio first, often by taking logs.
$\lim_{\lambda\to0}\dfrac{x^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}$ is $0/0$. Differentiate top and bottom with respect to $\lambda$: $\dfrac{x^\lambda\ln x}{1} \to \ln x$.
So the log is the $\lambda = 0$ member of the Box-Cox family, not a special case bolted on. Numerically, at $x = 5$ and $\lambda = 0.001$: $1.6107$ vs $\ln 5 = 1.6094$.

With $\rho = (\sigma-1)/\sigma$, $Y = [aL^\rho + (1-a)H^\rho]^{1/\rho}$. As $\sigma\to1$, $\rho\to0$, a $1^\infty$ form. Take logs: $\ln Y = \ln[aL^\rho + (1-a)H^\rho]/\rho$, now $0/0$. L'Hôpital in $\rho$:

- Using it when the form is not indeterminate.
- Differentiating the quotient with the quotient rule — differentiate numerator and denominator **separately**.

- **Econometrics**: [Box-Cox and Power Transformations](note:box-cox-and-power-transformations).
- **Labor / macro**: the Cobb-Douglas limit of the [CES Production Function](note:ces-production-function); why $\sigma = 1$ means constant factor shares.
- [Taylor Series Approximation](note:taylor-series-approximation) — an alternative route to most of these limits
